Not sure if this is a joke post, but on the off chance that it isn't... The hardware really won't make much difference unless you're unlucky enough for a vulnerability to be discovered in one of its components. I'm certain there are 'hardened' laptops on the market (i.e. used by military etc.), but such items tend to be inconvenient and overpriced for the average user. Most laptops come with a camera, which allows for MFA with appropriate software; however, biometrics are the weakest factor (as they can be easily harvested and never changed), so this generally adds very little security except against the most useless of would-be exploiters. The same can be said for thumb scanners (in fact, more often these are used to bypass security than reinforce it, in the cases I have seen). The general rule of thumb is: if someone has physical access to your machine, consider it already compromised.

Instead, if you're paranoid, focus your efforts on secure software and only ever use trusted networks.

Mozilla recently Open Sourced their Security Checklist for Workstations

Here is what they recommend on the hardware side:

  • System supports SecureBoot (ESSENTIAL)
  • System has no firewire, thunderbolt or ExpressCard ports (NICE)
  • System has a TPM chip (NICE)

Beware that this is for their specific threat model. You must adapt this to your own threat model. Also this does not include anything dealing with TEMPEST type unwanted emanations but there is no consumer product I'm aware of that addresses that anyway.

Additionally you might consider choosing Intel graphics chipset since that runs on open drivers without binary blobs.
